prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. Central separation guardrail Roads with six lanes or more in both directions shall have central separation facilities; green separation belts shall be preferred, and guardrail separation may be adopted where conditions are limited. The height of the central isolation guardrail shall be 110 cm. At openings where pedestrians cross, the guardrail height shall be gradually reduced to 70 cm; the length of the reduced section shall not be less than the stopping sight distance. Warning posts shall be set at the openings. 111 Figure 4.1-4 Example of flower-box central isolation guardrail B. Motor vehicle/non-motor vehicle separation guardrail On roads with four lanes or more in both directions, where the motor vehicle lane and non-motor vehicle lane are designed as a single roadway, separation guardrails shall be set between the motor vehicle lane and the non-motor vehicle lane. The height of the motor vehicle/non-motor vehicle separation guardrail shall be 90 cm. C. Pedestrian/non-pedestrian separation guardrail On road sections where the non-motor vehicle lane and sidewalk are on the same slab, and at intersections, commercial areas, schools, hospitals, and other sections with dense pedestrian flow where pedestrian crossing must be prevented, pedestrian/non-pedestrian separation guardrails shall be installed. The height of the pedestrian/non-pedestrian separation guardrail shall not be less than 90 cm. Where combined with flower boxes, anti-fall measures shall be provided. D. Sidewalk protective railing Where the embankment fill at bridgehead sections over rivers, roads, etc. is relatively high, or where there is a height difference between the outside of the sidewalk and the ground and there is a risk of pedestrians falling, sidewalk railings shall be installed along the outer edge of the sidewalk. The clear height of road sidewalk railings shall not be less than 110 cm. The clear height of sidewalk railings on the open side of bridges shall not be less than 110 cm. Where the open side of a bridge is a mixed pedestrian/non-motorized lane or a non-motorized lane, the clear height of the railing shall not be less than 140 cm. Railings that serve both as bridge anti-collision railings and sidewalk railings shall meet the technical requirements of both. E. Vehicle-blocking bollards At locations on urban roads where vehicles are not allowed to enter, when other measures cannot be adopted, vehicle-blocking bollards (vehicle-blocking stones) may be installed. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Vehicle Traffic System 2 Vehicle Traffic System 2.1 Vehicle Traffic Space Scale The longitudinal and transverse road space occupied by vehicular traffic is referred to as vehicle traffic space. Generally speaking, vehicle traffic space includes carriageways, bus-only lanes, medians, and roadside parking lanes. Figure 2.1-1 Components of Vehicle Traffic Space 2.1.1 Motor Vehicle Lane The width of a motor vehicle lane shall include the carriageway width and the curb lane widths on both sides. Where a single carriageway road or a three-carriageway road uses a central separator or double yellow lines to separate opposing traffic, the pavement width of the motor vehicle lane shall also include the width of the separator or double yellow lines. 1. Running Lane The width of a running lane is related to the road design speed. The recommended width for urban road running lanes is 3.25 m–3.5 m. 2. Two-Way Single Lane Where a lower-grade branch road is designed as a single lane permitting two-way travel, the width shall be 4.5 m. The subgrade width for sections with passing bays shall not be less than 6.5 m. 3. Bus-Only Lane The recommended width of a bus-only lane is 3.5 m. At bus stops, the lane width shall be 3 m. 27 Figure 2.1-2 Typical Lane Width Settings 2.1.2 Tidal Lane In response to the “tidal phenomenon” of traffic, lanes may be provided on road sections whose direction of travel can be changed according to traffic flow demand. In addition, the control center may monitor intersection conditions through instruments and, when appropriate, use remote control means to control signboards; where intersection signal controllers are connected in a computer network, they may also be identified through an automatic recognition system and automatically regulated. Figure 2.1-3 Tidal Lane and Movable Barrier 2.1.3 Shared Lane 1. The design concept of shared roads emphasizes the integration of sidewalk and motor vehicle lane space. The use of shared-road space is pedestrian-oriented. In terms of functional space, it meets the different needs of different groups, including walking, cycling, and motor vehicles. In terms of planning concept, shared roads emphasize people-centered design, serving pedestrians and providing convenience for urban residents, making them more willing to gather in shared-road spaces. Separation guardrails shall be provided with reflective markings to improve nighttime driving safety. On the premise of not encroaching upon the road construction clearance, separation guardrails on road sections may adopt a flower-box design. A. Central separation guardrail Roads with six lanes or more in both directions shall have central separation facilities; green separation belts shall be preferred, and guardrail separation may be adopted where conditions are limited. The height of the central isolation guardrail shall be 110 cm. At openings where pedestrians cross, the guardrail height shall be gradually reduced to 70 cm; the length of the reduced section shall not be less than the stopping sight distance. Warning posts shall be set at the openings. 111 Figure 4.1-4 Example of flower-box central isolation guardrail B. Motor vehicle/non-motor vehicle separation guardrail On roads with four lanes or more in both directions, where the motor vehicle lane and non-motor vehicle lane are designed as a single roadway, separation guardrails shall be set between the motor vehicle lane and the non-motor vehicle lane. The height of the motor vehicle/non-motor vehicle separation guardrail shall be 90 cm. C. Pedestrian/non-pedestrian separation guardrail On road sections where the non-motor vehicle lane and sidewalk are on the same slab, and at intersections, commercial areas, schools, hospitals, and other sections with dense pedestrian flow where pedestrian crossing must be prevented, pedestrian/non-pedestrian separation guardrails shall be installed. The height of the pedestrian/non-pedestrian separation guardrail shall not be less than 90 cm. Where combined with flower boxes, anti-fall measures shall be provided. D. Sidewalk protective railing Where the embankment fill at bridgehead sections over rivers, roads, etc. is relatively high, or where there is a height difference between the outside of the sidewalk and the ground and there is a risk of pedestrians falling, sidewalk railings shall be installed along the outer edge of the sidewalk. The clear height of road sidewalk railings shall not be less than 110 cm. The clear height of sidewalk railings on the open side of bridges shall not be less than 110 cm. Where the open side of a bridge is a mixed pedestrian/non-motorized lane or a non-motorized lane, the clear height of the railing shall not be less than 140 cm. Railings that serve both as bridge anti-collision railings and sidewalk railings shall meet the technical requirements of both. E. Vehicle-blocking bollards At locations on urban roads where vehicles are not allowed to enter, when other measures cannot be adopted, vehicle-blocking bollards (vehicle-blocking stones) may be installed. The installation of vehicle-blocking bollards (vehicle-blocking stones) shall comply with the following requirements: a. The installation of vehicle-blocking bollards (vehicle-blocking stones) shall be minimized; where installation is necessary, the style within the same area shall be unified. b. The spacing should be 1.3–1.5 m, and the height should be 0.4–0.6 m. c. To prevent injury caused by pedestrians or cyclists accidentally colliding at night, reflective film, warning lights, etc. shall be installed. 2. Anti-collision guardrails 112 A.
